claim: AIM § 7-6-16 defines thermal exhaust plumes from cooling towers as aviation hazards causing turbulence, vertical shear, reduced visibility, and engine contamination
source_title: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual § 7-6-16, Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes (Smoke Stacks and Cooling Towers)
supporting_excerpt: High temperature exhaust plumes can cause significant air disturbances such as turbulence and vertical shear. Other identified potential hazards include reduced visibility, oxygen depletion, engine particulate contamination, exposure to gaseous oxides, and/or icing. Results of encountering a plume may include airframe damage, aircraft upset, and engine damage or failure.
data_vintage: Current (AIM Basic with Change 1, 2, and 3, dated 9-5-24)
caveat: Cited via FAR/AIM.org reprint; primary source is FAA AIM

claim: Thermal plume hazards are most critical in approach and departure corridors, and turbulent effects extend more than 1,000 feet above the top of the stack or cooling tower
source_title: FAA Aeronautical Information Manual § 7-6-16, Avoid Flight in the Vicinity of Exhaust Plumes (Smoke Stacks and Cooling Towers)
supporting_excerpt: These hazards are most critical during low altitude flight in calm and cold air, especially in and around approach and departure corridors or airport traffic areas. Studies do predict that the significant turbulent effects of an exhaust plume can extend to heights of over 1,000 feet above the height of the top of the stack or cooling tower.

claim: AC 150/5200-33C requires stormwater detention basins near airports to remain totally dry between rainfalls; wet-bottom facilities attract hazardous wildlife into approach airspace
source_title: Advisory Circular 150/5200-33C, Hazardous Wildlife Attractants on or Near Airports
supporting_excerpt: Detention basins should remain totally dry between rainfalls, and where constant flow of water is anticipated through the basin, or where any portion of the basin bottom may remain wet, the detention facility should include a concrete or paved pad and/or ditch/swale in the bottom to prevent vegetation that may provide nesting habitat.

claim: Section 743 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 preserves full FAA ALP review authority for projects that materially impact safe and efficient aircraft operations, adversely affect ground safety, or adversely affect the value of prior federal investments
source_title: FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, Section 743 — Limited Regulation of Non-Federally Sponsored Property
supporting_excerpt: FAA retains authority to review and approve only those ALP changes that (1) materially impact the safe and efficient operation of aircraft at, to, or from the airport; (2) adversely affect the safety of people or property on the ground as a result of aircraft operations; or (3) adversely affect the value of prior Federal investments to a significant extent.
caveat: Content cited via AAAE regulatory alert summary and AirTAP briefing; language confirmed consistent across sources

claim: Emergency diesel generators used by data centers emit NOx, CO, particulate matter, and volatile organic compounds, and require air quality permits
source_title: Frequently Asked Air Questions (FAAQs): Understanding Data Center Emergency Generators and Their Air Permits — Williams Mullen
supporting_excerpt: Generators emit several regulated pollutants during fuel combustion, including nitrogen oxides (NOx), carbon monoxide (CO), particulate matter (PM), and volatile organic compounds (VOCs). They may also release hazardous air pollutants like formaldehyde and benzene depending on fuel type and engine design.
caveat: No specific aviation impact discussed in source; PM and smoke emissions are relevant to the AC 150/5300-13B RPZ smoke-generating prohibition

claim: Prince William County supervisors voted 8-0 to deny the Dulles Cloud South 2,000-acre data center project in July 2026 following community opposition and court reversals of prior rezonings
source_title: Prince William Co. supervisors deny 2,000-acre Dulles South data center plans — WTOP News
supporting_excerpt: The Prince William County Board of Supervisors voted 8-0 to reject the Dulles Cloud South data center project near Catharpin. The board had approved three rezoning applications in December 2023, but residents and the American Battlefield Trust sued, and a Prince William County court threw out all rezonings in 2025, which was backed up by the Virginia Court of Appeals in March.
airport_or_entity: Prince William County, VA / Dulles South
caveat: This project is off-airport property (not on MWAA land); context value is showing regional data center regulatory friction, not direct precedent for on-airport regulation
